---
title: "Air Conductor"
sidebarTitle: "Air Conductor"
description: "Oxygen's durable task engine, which queues background work in Postgres and runs it to completion through restarts and deploys"
---

**Air Conductor** is Oxygen's durable task engine. It runs the work that
happens after a request returns, such as
[Airway](/guide/build/data-infrastructure/airway) loads into
[Airhouse](/guide/build/data-infrastructure/airhouse), automation runs, and
scheduled agents, and it keeps that work going when a process stops partway
through. Where [Airform](/guide/build/data-infrastructure/airform) shapes
tables, Air Conductor decides when work runs and makes sure it finishes. It
has three parts:

- A **queue** in Oxygen's own Postgres database, where every piece of work is
  written down before anything starts it.
- **Workers**, which claim work from the queue and run it. They run inside
  `oxy serve` by default, or as a separate fleet started with `oxy worker`.
- A **scheduler**, which turns schedules, monitor scans, and pre-aggregation
  refreshes into queued work when they come due.

<Frame caption="Work is recorded in Postgres before any worker runs it, so a worker that stops never takes the work with it: another worker claims it, and the run continues from the steps already finished.">

## Why it matters

- **Work survives restarts.** A deploy, a crash, or a lost node never drops
  queued work. Each run keeps a record of the steps it has finished, so after a
  restart it continues from there instead of starting over.
- **No extra service to run.** The queue lives in the same Postgres database
  Oxygen already uses. To scale out, you add workers, with no message broker
  to deploy alongside them.
- **One engine for background work.** Airway runs,
  [automations](/guide/build/automations), scheduled agents, pre-aggregation
  refreshes, and scheduled [Oxy Functions](/guide/build/sdk/functions) all
  queue and recover the same way.
- **You can see it.** The **Orchestrator Dashboard** in Oxygen Factory lists
  active and recent runs, shows each run's tree of steps, and can retry a run
  that failed. It replaced the older Coordinator view.

## How it runs

- **In-process by default, a fleet when you need one.** `oxy serve` runs
  workers inside the server process, so a single instance handles everything
  on its own. To scale background work separately, start one or more
  `oxy worker` processes against the same database and turn off in-process
  workers on the serving tier with `--no-workers` (or `OXY_ROLE=serve`). Each
  worker runs up to 32 tasks at once, which you can change with
  `OXY_WORKER_MAX_INFLIGHT`.
- **New work starts in milliseconds, or within 10 seconds.** A Postgres
  notification wakes an idle worker as soon as work is queued. If the
  notification is missed, workers find the work on their next poll, at most
  10 seconds later. A connection pooler in transaction mode silently drops
  these notifications, so if work keeps starting about 10 seconds late, check
  the pooler before anything else.
- **Two kinds of worker, switched on and off separately.** Queue workers run
  work that is already queued. The scheduler decides when scheduled work is due
  and queues it. The scheduler runs in every Oxygen process except a stateless
  serving replica, and `OXY_INPROC_GLOBAL_WORKER=0` turns it off. Turning off
  queue workers doesn't stop the scheduler, and turning off the scheduler
  doesn't stop queue workers. If no process runs the scheduler, you can still
  create and edit schedules, but none of them ever fires.
- **Each scheduled time fires once.** Running the scheduler on several
  instances is safe, because only one of them claims a given due time. If no
  scheduler was running through several scheduled times, the schedule fires
  once when one starts again, then continues from the next future time. It
  does not replay every missed run.
- **A stopped worker's work returns in about 90 seconds.** Workers send a
  heartbeat while they run a task. If the heartbeats stop for 60 seconds, the
  claim expires, and a check that runs every 30 seconds puts the task back in
  the queue for another worker. A worker shutting down cleanly, as in a
  deploy, hands its tasks back at once. A task whose worker dies three times
  is marked dead instead of being tried again, so a task that crashes its
  worker can't take down the fleet one worker at a time.
- **Recovery can repeat a step.** A run continues from its last finished step,
  so a step that was partway through when its worker stopped runs again from
  the beginning. Write steps that call external APIs or write data so they are
  safe to run twice. A run that still hasn't finished after four recoveries is
  marked failed. Retrying it from the Orchestrator Dashboard starts it again
  with a fresh count.
- **Retries are opt-in.** Recovery, which happens when a worker stops, is not
  the same as a retry, which happens when a task fails. The engine retries a
  failed task only when the feature that queued it asked for retries. Otherwise
  the run reports the error. A cancelled task is never retried, and cancelling
  a run cancels its steps too.
- **Waiting has a limit, except when it waits for a person.** A step waiting
  for the work it started times out after 4 hours and finishes as
  `timed_out`. A run waiting for a human answer waits as long as it takes, and
  it keeps a worker slot the whole time.

## Where it fits

The engine sits underneath the features that start background work, and
each of them adds its own rules on top. [Airway](/guide/build/data-infrastructure/airway/pipelines)
allows one run per pipeline per workspace, and
[automations](/guide/build/automations/task-types) run each task as a queued
step, so a run interrupted partway through resumes at the step it was on. For which parts of a
deployment stay up during a restart, see
[High availability](/guide/manage/high-availability).
